articleTitle: Developments in the field of extra-high voltage
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: World energy consumption and its electrical part are indicated. Choice of transmission voltage with regard to distance, load and other factors is discussed. Technical problems in connection with extra-high voltages, especially Insulation, corona losses and radio interference, reactive power and voltage regulation, and stability are considered. A description of the Canadian 735-kV system and the experience from the field tests and operation are given. Future development in the extra-high tension field is forecast and some comparisons between ac and dc are drawn.

articleTitle: People, principles and progress in electrical power
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: In the public mind electrical engineering is thought of mainly as a mixture of hard metals and hard logic; in fact, as a cold and soulless activity, appropriate only to ‘boffins’ and back-room boys. It is believed to be devoid of imaginative and emotional appeal and — in the classical sense of the word — is thought not to be a humane subject. The proper study of mankind is man, as educationists are fond of insisting; and to this view are added the false ideas that engineering is not about men, but only about things, and that the humane factors in engineering are trivial. Nothing could be further from the truth.

articleTitle: A review of electrical engineering contributions to medicine
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The object of this paper is to provide a survey of some of the major advances made in the realm of electrical engineering applied to medicine. The main accent is upon instrumentation and devices used in cardiology. A brief history of electrocardiography is presented and plethysmography (volume flow measurement), electromyography (muscle activity measurement) and endoradiosonde (telemetering capsules) devices are dealt with. An engineering view is adopted in the explanation of some of the physiological mechanisms. Finally some general remarks are made about education in this sphere of activity.

abstract: Alongside of jokes about mothers-in-law and the British workman, the boffin or egghead has always, and still does, come in for his share. This is probably one of the reasons why the research worker's image in the practical engineer's eye is just about as weak as that of the engineer himself in the public eye. The major reason in both cases is the same — the man in the street never meets, never hears about, and is hardly aware of the engineer, although almost everything he does and uses rests on engineering. That is to say, he is very much aware of the products of engineering, but not of the engineer. In much the same way, many engineers use and seek the products of research, without being aware of the persons responsible for doing the research.

articleTitle: Some basic problems encountered in South Africa in the planning of a comprehensive broadcast coverage scheme
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Before an approach can be made to the overall design of a network of broadcast transmitters capable of giving coverage to any country, the various factors that will be encountered in that country have to be specified, analysed and evaluated. History, on a world-wide basis, has shown that the approach made in the past was often mistaken, in that not all the problematical factors were known or correctly evaluated, nor were certain possible methods of solution then adequately developed. Political and other civic evolution of the masses, in more, recent years, has imposed problems on the broadcaster that were unknown or hardly noticeable as little as 10 years ago. The setting up of more erudite communications systems throughout the world has led to the very rapid dissemination of news and other information. This has taken place on official news service circuits and on both fully subversive and quasi-subversive (propaganda) communication channels. The challenges that this speeding up of the spread of information, both true and false, has posed for any government and for the public service broadcast authority of that country are considerable. The growth of the problems that have arisen as a consequence of modern telecommunication development has led to the necessity of every broadcasting authority in the world being forced today to establish and operate very closeknit and expensive national broadcast networks of high technical excellence. In addition, the simultaneous rise in the demands made by the average listener for an ever better signal-to-noise ratio at his receiver output has become one of the major challenges of a purely technical nature.
